title: India Sweetens Incentives for City Gas Firms as LPG-to-PNG Migration Accelerates
excerpt: New scheme offers cheaper domestic gas to distributors for every household they connect, as India races to cut LPG imports amid the West Asia supply crisis.
body:
• India now offers city gas distributors 200 standard cubic metres of cheaper domestic gas for every household that starts using piped natural gas (PNG), effective September 2026.
  • The incentive is expected to cut the payback period for new PNG connections from roughly 10 years to about three, boosting company margins and network expansion.
  • India has 17.4 million PNG connections against 331.4 million active LPG households — the government aims to reach 50 million PNG connections by 2030.
  • LPG under-recovery stands at ₹690 per domestic cylinder, translating into annual losses of about ₹1.38 trillion for oil marketing companies.

India has announced a fresh incentive scheme for city gas distribution companies to accelerate the migration of households from liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cylinders to piped natural gas (PNG), Reuters reported on August 18. The move is the latest in a series of increasingly aggressive policy actions as the West Asia conflict continues to disrupt fuel shipments and inflate import costs.

Under the new scheme, effective September, city gas distributors will receive an additional 200 standard cubic metres of cheaper, domestically produced gas for every household they connect that begins actively using and paying for piped natural gas, according to the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.

A Shrinking Payback Window

The extra allocation of domestic gas — priced well below imported liquefied natural gas — is designed to lower the overall sourcing costs for distributors and make new connections commercially viable. The government estimates the scheme will help companies recoup their investment in new household connections in about three years, down from roughly 10 years under previous economics.

Shares of major city gas distributors rallied following the announcement. Indraprastha Gas climbed 3.5 per cent, Mahanagar Gas gained 4 per cent, and Gujarat Energy rose 0.5 per cent, reflecting market confidence in the programme's potential to drive earnings growth.

"Field experience indicates that access constraints, consumer non-responsiveness and local issues have limited the effectiveness [of PNG adoption]."

— Neeraj Mittal, Petroleum Secretary

Why India Wants Kitchens Off LPG

India is the world's second-largest LPG importer, shipping in about 22 million metric tonnes in 2025 at a cost of nearly $12 billion, mostly from the Middle East. Approximately 60 per cent of India's LPG is imported, with nearly 90 per cent of those shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz — now a conflict zone following hostilities between the United States, Israel, and Iran.

The vulnerability is not theoretical. Oil marketing companies currently face an under-recovery of ₹690 on every domestic LPG cylinder, translating into annual losses of about ₹1.38 trillion, Livemint reported, citing Petroleum Secretary Neeraj Mittal's letter to state chief secretaries. The government also provides a ₹300 per cylinder subsidy to households under the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana, adding another ₹19,000 crore in annual expenditure.

By contrast, PNG is delivered through fixed underground pipelines fed from diverse sources — domestic fields and multiple import terminals — making it far more resilient to global shocks. In major metros, PNG is roughly 12 to 15 per cent cheaper than non-subsidised LPG, and households pay only for what they consume, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

The Scale of the Task

India currently has about 17.4 million domestic PNG connections against 331.4 million active household LPG customers as of July 1, according to government data cited by Reuters. The gap is enormous, but the government estimates that around 60 lakh (6 million) LPG consumers already live in areas where PNG infrastructure exists, making them immediate candidates for migration.

Since the policy push began in March 2026 with the Natural Gas and Petroleum Products Distribution Order — issued under the Essential Commodities Act — the government has taken increasingly forceful steps. Households in areas with existing PNG infrastructure were given a 90-day window to switch. In May, the government barred PNG-connected households from refilling LPG cylinders with immediate effect and reduced the number of subsidised cylinders under the Ujjwala scheme from nine to four.

The infrastructure rollout is concentrated in northern and western states — Delhi-NCR, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and Maharashtra — but is expanding into South India through Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana. City gas distribution coverage has grown from 57 geographical areas in 2014 to over 300 today.

What Indian Diaspora Households Should Know

For NRI families with property in India, the transition has practical implications. Households in pipeline-served areas that have not switched to PNG risk losing their LPG connections. Family members managing kitchens in metro areas should check whether their locality falls within a city gas distribution zone and apply for a PNG connection before the enforcement tightens further.

Looking Ahead

The government's target is ambitious: 50 million domestic PNG connections by 2030, more than tripling the current base. The September incentive scheme, combined with the stick of LPG discontinuation, suggests the Centre is prepared to use both carrots and regulatory force to drive the transition. Whether the pipeline infrastructure can keep pace with the policy ambition — particularly in congested urban areas where right-of-way approvals have historically stalled projects — remains the central question.
nri_angle: NRI families with property in Indian metros risk losing LPG connections if they do not switch to piped natural gas where infrastructure is available.
